consensus_summary: In apocalyptic usage the symbolic beast/wild animal stands for brutal anti-God political power—kingdoms, empires or rulers that oppose God and persecute the saints (Daniel’s four beasts; Revelation’s sea/land/scarlet beasts), with secondary readings as Antichrist, Rome/Nero, papacy, timeless evil, or (minority) degraded human nature.
book_summary: A nation or kingdom organized under earthly rule, often depicted in wild/predatory character; different beasts mark different kingdoms, while clean versus unclean beasts mark kinds of people.
consensus_core_identification: God-opposing earthly kingdoms/empires/rulers (political powers animated by satanic arrogance)
book_core_identification: earthly nation or kingdom (frequently predatory) plus clean/unclean animals as kinds of people
boundary_disagreement: Consensus centers the referent on anti-God/oppressive character and largely confines it to apocalyptic empires/rulers; the book drops opposition-to-God as definitional (retaining only ‘often’ predatory), applies the symbol to any earthly kingdom, and explicitly adds clean/unclean beasts as a classification of people (Acts 10).
material_contradiction: None; the book does not deny the anti-God kingdom cases that form the consensus core.
rationale: Minimum cores both identify beasts with kingdoms/nations (explicitly supported by Dan 7:17; 8:20-21). The book therefore preserves the consensus referent rather than replacing it. It nevertheless materially widens extension and softens boundaries by (a) omitting necessary opposition to God and (b) elevating the clean/unclean-people reading (present only as a minority alternative in the consensus) to co-equal status. This is classic refinement by broadening, not equivalence, contradiction, or novelty.
strongest_objection: The consensus treats ‘opposition to God / persecution’ as essential to the symbol; the book’s neutral ‘earthly rule, often predatory’ plus people-classification therefore under-specifies the dominant biblical usage.
